chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar from Muhammad ibn Isma'il from Ali ibn al-Nu'man from Sa'id al-A'raj from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about two men who were milk-brothers, who were brought from the land of polytheism. One of them said to the other, 'You are my brother,' and they were recognized as such. Then they were freed and remained affirming the brotherhood. Then one of them died. He said, 'The inheritance goes to the other; they are believed.'

key_terms.حَمِيلَيْنِ: Two men who are milk-brothers or sworn brothers
key_terms.يُصَدَّقَانِ: They are believed (their testimony is accepted)

ai.seo_question: What is the inheritance ruling for two men who recognized each other as brothers while in a land of polytheism?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies that sworn or milk-brotherhood (*ikha'*) established in the pre-Islamic or early Islamic period creates a valid inheritance link, provided both parties affirm the bond. The phrase 'they are verified' (*yusaddaqan*) indicates that their mutual testimony is sufficient evidence for the heir to claim the estate, reflecting the juristic principle that *ikha'* can substitute for blood relation in inheritance matters. This ruling highlights the flexibility of Shia fiqh in recognizing social bonds formed through mutual consent and public acknowledgment.
